questions.q: In which year was the Battle of Talikota fought, and what was the alternative name for this battle mentioned in the NCERT text?
questions.a: The Battle of Talikota was fought in 1565 and is also called the Battle of Rakshasi-Tangadi. A wrong answer (e.g., 1526, 1576, or "Battle of Panipat") reveals the student is conflating this battle with other major battles in Indian history or has not memorised the specific date — a basic recall error that makes chronological analysis impossible.

questions.q: Why did the Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda) form an alliance against Vijayanagara in 1565, despite having fought among themselves previously?
questions.a: The Sultanates allied because Rama Raya's policy of intervening in their succession disputes and playing one against the other threatened their collective survival; they recognised that Vijayanagara's divide-and-rule strategy would eventually eliminate them all. A wrong answer focusing only on "religious differences" or "territorial ambition" misses the specific diplomatic trigger — Rama Raya's adventurous policy — and reflects the common misconception that the conflict was primarily religious rather than geopolitical.

questions.q: Rama Raya was not the king of Vijayanagara in 1565. What was his official position, and how did this affect the chain of command during the battle?
questions.a: Rama Raya was the chief minister (de facto ruler) acting on behalf of the nominal emperor Sadashiva Raya of the Aravidu lineage; his authority depended on controlling the amara-nayaka commanders, some of whom may have hesitated to obey a minister over the king. A wrong answer stating he was "the king" or "a nayaka" reveals confusion about the Vijayanagara political structure (covered in node 003 and 004) and prevents understanding why the central authority collapsed so rapidly after his death.

questions.q: Compare the Vijayanagara-Sultanate relations under Krishnadeva Raya (1509-1529) with those under Rama Raya (1542-1565). What specific shift in diplomatic strategy explains the different outcomes?
questions.a: Krishnadeva Raya maintained a balance of power — supporting claimants in Sultanates to keep them stable but not weak, and accepting Sultan of Bijapur's mediation in Vijayanagara succession — whereas Rama Raya actively destabilised Sultanates by backing rival claimants simultaneously, provoking a defensive coalition. A wrong answer claiming "relations were always hostile" ignores the textual evidence of cooperation (Krishnadeva Raya's title "establisher of the Yavana kingdom") and fails to analyse diplomacy as a variable.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The Battle of Talikota destroyed the Vijayanagara Empire." Use evidence from the NCERT text to support your judgment.
questions.a: The statement is partially true but misleading: the battle destroyed the *imperial capital* and *centralised imperial authority*, but the Vijayanagara political tradition survived through the Aravidu dynasty (ruling from Penukonda/Chandragiri) and, more enduringly, through the nayaka kingdoms (Madurai, Thanjavur, Ikkeri, Mysore) that continued Vijayanagara's administrative and architectural traditions. A wrong answer treating the battle as a total endpoint misses the distinction between "empire as centralised state" and "empire as cultural-political tradition" — a key historiographical nuance for board and competitive exams.

questions.q: Construct a cause-effect chain with at least four links showing how the geography of the Deccan (river valleys, terrain, horse trade routes) contributed to the conflict between Vijayanagara and the Sultanates culminating in Talikota.
questions.a: A strong chain: (1) The Krishna-Tungabhadra doab (Raichur doab) was a fertile, contested zone controlling revenue and troop movement → (2) Control of west coast ports (Goa, Bhatkal) was essential for horse imports from Arabia/Persia → (3) The Deccan Sultanates and Vijayanagara both needed horses for cavalry, creating structural rivalry over trade routes → (4) The rocky terrain of the Deccan made fortified cities (Gulbarga, Bidar, Bijapur, Vijayanagara) the keys to territorial control, encouraging a siege-warfare logic that favoured large coalitions. A weak chain lists geography facts without linking them to political-military causality.
